es.meaning: To talk to someone who isn't listening or won't be persuaded, so the words go nowhere.
es.example: Le he explicado tres veces cómo funciona y sigue sin entenderlo; es como hablar con la pared.
es.exampleTranslation: I've explained how it works three times and he still doesn't get it — it's like talking to a wall.

it.literal: it's like talking to the wall
it.meaning: To speak to someone who won't listen or refuses to be swayed — words that hit an unmoving surface.
it.example: Gli ho ripetuto mille volte di stare attento, ma è come parlare al muro.
it.exampleTranslation: I've told him a thousand times to be careful, but it's like talking to a wall.

bridge.note: Rare case: the same wall in both languages, doing the same job. Both reach for a mute, unmoving physical surface to describe a listener who won't be reached. Low interference risk — this is one of the few genuine one-to-one calques in the bank.

review.notes: Banked 2026-07-24. Italian side sourced from @learnandloveitalian (Instagram), run by Joe's Italian teacher — confirmed native Italian speaker, treated as a strong discovery source, not a citation on its own. Formal citation is Accademia della Crusca's dedicated article tracing the phrase to the 14th century — about as authoritative as Italian etymology gets. Spanish side has no formal RAE headword; sourced to real, heavy colloquial usage (Corpus tier, same as 0002's balcone entry) — genuinely current but not academy-listed. Meaning and both examples written fresh. Needs native review on both sides. Source-authority note: cited as 'Corpus' because Accademia della Crusca (the actual page checked) isn't in the schema's fixed authority list — it is not Treccani, and labelling it as Treccani would claim a page that was never fetched. Crusca is, if anything, a stronger authority than the schema has a slot for.
